presentingComplaint: Rapidly progressive painful red swollen right lower leg for 24 hours with high fever and shaking chills; referred from primary care as suspected deep vein thrombosis.
history: Previously well apart from chronic venous insufficiency and a healed interdigital fungal fissure of the right foot. Woke the previous morning with an abrupt shaking chill followed by fever to 39°C, then noticed a hot red patch over the right shin that expanded over hours with a burning, tight sensation. Because the leg was unilaterally swollen, warm and tender, her GP calculated a Wells score of 2 and sent her for an urgent venous Doppler, which was negative for DVT; a D-dimer had been mildly elevated. No recent immobilisation, long-haul travel, surgery, oral contraceptive use or prior VTE. No trauma or animal/insect bite. No dyspnoea or pleuritic chest pain. No diabetes. Denies pus, blackening of skin or pain grossly out of proportion. She recalls a small itchy crack between the fourth and fifth toes for a fortnight (tinea pedis) as the likely portal of entry.
examination: Alert, uncomfortable but not toxic. Right leg: a fiery, bright-red, oedematous plaque over the anteromedial shin with a SHARPLY DEMARCATED, palpably RAISED border with a visible step-off from normal skin (peau d'orange surface), warm and tender; erythema advancing since marking 6 hours earlier. No skin necrosis, no haemorrhagic bullae, no crepitus, and pain is proportionate to examination. Tender enlarged right inguinal lymph nodes and a faint ascending lymphangitic streak up the medial thigh. Interdigital maceration/fissuring between right 4th-5th toes. Calf soft, non-tense; Homan's non-contributory; peripheral pulses intact. Cardiorespiratory and abdominal exam unremarkable.
imaging: Whole-leg compression venous ultrasound Doppler: fully compressible deep veins, no thrombus - DVT excluded. Soft-tissue US of the plaque: dermal oedema with hyperechoic subcutaneous fat and NO cobblestoning/deep fluid collection and no gas; findings confined to the dermis/superficial subcutis, no drainable abscess.
microbiology: Blood cultures x2 sent (low yield expected, <5% positive in erysipelas). Skin swab of interdigital fissure. No abscess to aspirate. Group A beta-haemolytic Streptococcus (Streptococcus pyogenes) is the presumed pathogen given the sharply marginated lesion, lymphangitis and rising ASO titre.
differentialDiagnoses: Deep vein thrombosis (initial referral diagnosis - excluded by negative compression Doppler)
Cellulitis (deeper, poorly-demarcated margins - distinguished by the raised sharply demarcated border here)
Early necrotizing fasciitis (excluded: no pain out of proportion, no bullae/crepitus, non-toxic, normal lactate)
Stasis dermatitis / lipodermatosclerosis of chronic venous insufficiency (usually bilateral, afebrile, chronic)
finalDiagnosis: Erysipelas of the right lower leg (superficial group A streptococcal dermal infection) with tinea pedis as portal of entry; DVT excluded.
citations: IDSA - Practice Guidelines for the Diagnosis and Management of Skin and Soft Tissue Infections - 2014
Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22e - Cellulitis, Necrotizing Fasciitis, and Subcutaneous Tissue Infections (streptococcal skin infection)
stewardship: Non-purulent, non-severe streptococcal skin infection: narrow-spectrum beta-lactam targeting Streptococcus pyogenes. Access-tier agent (penicillin/amoxicillin) preferred; no anti-MRSA or anti-pseudomonal cover indicated. Anticoagulation is NOT warranted once DVT is excluded. Treat concurrent tinea pedis (topical antifungal) and elevate the limb to reduce recurrence.
contraindications: Avoid unnecessary empirical anticoagulation once compression Doppler excludes DVT
Avoid broad-spectrum/anti-MRSA therapy (e.g., vancomycin) for non-purulent erysipelas without risk factors
In documented penicillin anaphylaxis, substitute a macrolide (clarithromycin) or clindamycin
edgeCases: Unilateral hot swollen leg overlaps clinically with DVT - bilateral leg erythema with fever is more often bilateral cellulitis mimics/stasis dermatitis than true infection
Failure of the raised margin to advance and presence of fluctuance/pain out of proportion should prompt reassessment for abscess or necrotizing fasciitis
Interdigital tinea/fissuring is a common overlooked portal of entry and a driver of recurrence
expectedMaiK: Fever with rigors plus a sharply demarcated, raised, brightly erythematous plaque and ascending lymphangitis is erysipelas, not DVT - a negative compression Doppler excludes the referral diagnosis and the lesion margin distinguishes it from deeper cellulitis.
expectedNextQuestions: Is there a portal of entry (tinea pedis, fissure, ulcer, insect bite)?
Is the erythematous border sharply demarcated and raised (erysipelas) or diffuse (cellulitis)?
Any features of necrotizing infection - pain out of proportion, bullae, crepitus, rapid systemic deterioration?
Any DVT risk factors or prior VTE, and what did the venous Doppler show?
expectedInvestigations: Compression venous Doppler ultrasound of the leg (exclude DVT)
Mark the erythema border to monitor progression
regressionAssertions: Engine must return ERYSIPELAS as the top diagnosis despite unilateral leg swelling and calf tenderness suggestive of DVT.
dvt must appear only as a differential and be down-ranked by the negative compression Doppler and the sharply demarcated raised border.
Recommended empiric therapy must be a narrow-spectrum anti-streptococcal beta-lactam (penicillin/amoxicillin), not anti-MRSA or anti-pseudomonal cover.
Anticoagulation must NOT be recommended once DVT is excluded.
